messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Jason Latu, a 39‑year‑old Pacific Islander airline pilot, was a routine, disciplined man before the night that would reshape his life. On a rain‑slick evening in January, he was pulled over on a quiet county road for a broken taillight. The police officer, a tall white man with a no‑smile face, stepped out of the patrol car and demanded Jason’s license and registration. Jason’s hands trembled, the engine’s hum seemed louder than ever, and a sudden nausea gnawed at his stomach. The officer’s proximity—his very close stance—made the air feel thick. When the officer’s badge flashed, Jason’s mind jumped to the worst scenario: a confrontation, a weapon fired, or a handcuff. That immediate threat spurred an internal alarm that magnified every sensation: the vibration of the steering wheel, the scent of the officer’s after‑shave, the faint echo of the distant siren. Jason’s proximity to the officer and his own bodily discomfort together produced a heightened sense of threat. The officer’s stance, a trigger in itself, fed back into Jason’s perception of danger; he could not separate the physical closeness from the fear it ignited. The panic he felt in that moment left a scar that would haunt him even when he was miles away from that small road. A month later, Jason sat at the kitchen table, nursing a cup of coffee, and the memory surged with brutal clarity. He could see the officer’s face, hear the click of the key on the dashboard, feel the engine’s tremor. The memory felt more real than the mundane memories of family dinners, and the terror he felt then had returned, uninvited, whenever he closed his eyes. This vivid recollection became a trigger: the thought of a police stop would launch him into that same panic, the same nausea, the same belief that delays meant imminent danger. In turn, the persistent threat he sensed—fear that any pause in the flow of traffic or time would invite attack—made the memory even more vivid. The terror on recall and the belief that something bad would happen whenever something took longer than expected reinforced each other. Each time he imagined a delay, the memory flared, and the memory’s intensity magnified his threat perception. When Jason resumed flying, the aircraft became a second battlefield. Every long haul was filled with proximity to strangers—passengers, crew, and strangers on the runway. The mere sound of a child’s cry or a passing engine hiss set his heart racing, and he would jump, his body reacting to ordinary sounds that would not disturb most people. In the cockpit, a sudden delay, a weather delay, or a minute’s hold at an intersection was enough to trigger his internal alarm. The startle responses to ordinary noises and the sense of threat from strangers approached him even in everyday airport interactions. As the threat lingered, Jason’s avoidance grew; he avoided longer flights, avoided engaging with cabin crew during layovers, and began to distance himself from his wife, whose support he could no longer face. The consequences spilled into his marriage, contributing to the divorce he would file two years later. The accumulation of these cycles left Jason exhausted and isolated. He could no longer breathe the normal rhythm of flight. He started experiencing bouts of nausea on the ground, even when not near an aircraft, simply at the sight of a police badge or the sound of a door closing. The terror he felt when driving with others—the idea that any second might hold a threat—forced him to cancel weekend trips. Jason’s fear of delay made him hyper‑vigilant, and the memory of that night kept returning, each time making the threat seem even more imminent. This tightening loop had become the backdrop of his life: the threat of a delay feeding the memory, the memory feeding triggers, the triggers feeding threat. Now, at 39, Jason sits in a therapist’s office for the first time, his hands clenched around a pen, the surface of the chair too cold to stay. The decision to seek help came after a near‑miss on a short flight where a sudden delay and a low‑volume alarm caused him to panic to the point of nearly aborting the landing. What frightens him most is the possibility that he will never feel safe in the cockpit again, that the memory will never recede, and that his life will stay trapped in this loop of threat and panic. Yet he also holds a fragile hope: that through understanding his triggers, he can regain the calm he once had, that the memory can become a story, not a terror, and that he might once again find safety in the rhythm of flight.
